title: IFT-BioSim
text:
A national target is one number. The farms that have to meet it are thousands of different businesses, and the same target can cost one of them very little and another a great deal. IFT-BioSim asks how a common national transition objective can create very different economic pressures across heterogeneous farms.
It focuses on who bears adjustment, who responds, and how policy design changes incidence.

Why it matters
A technically feasible national pathway does not reveal how costly the transition may be for particular farms. IFT-BioSim is designed to make that distribution visible and to test whether alternative compensation or incentive designs change the burden.

title: About
text:
I am Elvis Kwame Ofori, a Ghanaian researcher and writer based in Ireland.
My path has run from Ghana to China and now Ireland, and moving between those places has shaped how I think about policy. National decisions look very different once they reach households, farms, firms and communities, and that difference is what I study and write about.
The longer story: How I got here is a living account of the places, people and opportunities that shaped the work I do and the questions I now write about.

title: About
text:
What I write about
This website is broader than my PhD. I use the blog to think through public policy, economics, science, technology, agriculture and food, Ghana and Africa, Ireland, the United States, books, research life and things I have noticed along the way. Some posts argue a case, some explain, and some are simply an attempt to make sense of something I have read, seen or experienced.

title: About
text:
Research
I am a PhD Researcher and Research Assistant in Plant & AgriBiosciences at the University of Galway’s Ryan Institute. My doctoral work asks who actually carries the adjustment when a country sets agricultural, climate and land-use targets: which farms, which production systems and which places.
I work within the wider FUSION and FORESIGHT modelling environment at the University of Galway. My doctoral research is supervised by David Styles and Cathal O’Donoghue.

title: About

Editorial standards
EKO Perspectives is a personal publication. I use public sources wherever possible and link directly to the evidence behind factual claims. I do not publish confidential, restricted, unpublished or under-review research results belonging to me or collaborators.
Where an affiliation, funder or research relationship is relevant to a post, I disclose it. If I make a substantive correction after publication, I note the correction and the date on the post. The aim is to keep a clear line between public evidence, my interpretation of it, and work that is not yet public.

title: How I got here
text:
Elvis Kwame Ofori standing outdoors in a patterned cardigan.
I studied accounting in Ghana, and I now build agricultural and land-use models in Ireland. Neither the start nor the middle was planned. This page is the longer version of how one led to the other, and an attempt to give some credit to the people and places that made the route possible. The About page has the short version.
Looking back makes the path look neater than it was. I studied accounting in Accra, did National Service with the National Petroleum Authority and was posted to Takoradi. A scholarship took me to northern China, where research pulled me towards policy, sustainability and energy. Another turn brought me to Ireland, to agriculture and land use, and to the farmers who live with decisions made a long way from their land.
I have never read the opportunities I received as proof that I was the most exceptional person in the room. There were people more brilliant than me. What I did learn was to be ready when a door opened, to make hay, as the old saying goes, while the sun shines. And very little of it happened alone. Teachers, family, friends, colleagues and supervisors opened doors, gave advice, trusted me with responsibility, or simply made an unfamiliar place feel less strange. This page is partly my attempt to remember them, and I expect to keep adding to it.

title: How I got here
text:
Ghana: where it began
I studied Accounting at the University of Professional Studies, Accra. It looks some distance from the work I do now, but I do not think of it as an abandoned beginning. Accounting taught me to pay attention to numbers and organisations, and to the difference between what something appears to be and what the underlying records actually show. It took me years to see how useful that instinct would become.
After university I did my National Service with Ghana’s National Petroleum Authority. I had been living in Accra, and the posting sent me to Takoradi, one of the first times life moved me somewhere I had not planned to go. Takoradi was also my first taste of real responsibility. I worked nights and double shifts, and I was trusted to supervise. It was not glamorous, but it was an education of its own. University had taught me concepts; work began to show me what happens when procedures, rules and decisions meet the people who have to carry them out, and how differently one organisation looks depending on where inside it you stand.
I would not have called any of that an interest in policy implementation at the time. But the question stayed with me, and a few years later it came back as research: one of my early papers, published in Resources Policy, looked at how to measure safety performance in Ghana’s oil and gas industry.

title: How I got here
section: China: learning to think in frameworks
text:
China: learning to think in frameworks
In 2019 I received a full scholarship for an MSc in Management Science and Engineering and moved to Taiyuan, in northern China. I knew China would be different. I was less prepared for how different the north would feel to someone arriving from Ghana, and the cold introduced itself quickly.
The larger change was intellectual. China was where I learned to approach problems through frameworks. Instead of seeing only a result, I started asking what structure produced it. Who were the actors? What assumptions sat underneath the analysis, and what evidence was it using? What happened when a policy moved off the page and into an economy or a community? My research ranged across sustainability, development, environmental policy and energy economics. Energy held my attention because its decisions were so large: governments, industries and major firms could change what happened across a whole system, and thinking at that scale taught me to look for the links between institutions, incentives and outcomes. I later began doctoral study in China as well.



With people who were part of my life in China.


China became much more than a scholarship or a degree. The people around me became part of the education too.
Part of my life there never appeared on a transcript. I taught English as a second language to Chinese students, and I especially enjoyed the younger learners. I still love watching someone grow more confident as something that looked difficult begins to make sense. The same instinct carried into my work with colleagues. When someone was struggling with an analysis, I liked sitting down with them and working through it: not which button to press, but what the numbers were saying and whether the interpretation held up. I have come to think of data analysis almost as a conversation. You learn how to talk to data. You also have to learn when to stop talking long enough to let the data answer back.
That pleasure in teaching and explaining has followed me into almost everything I have done since.

title: How I got here
section: Ireland: bringing the question closer to the ground
text:
Ireland: bringing the question closer to the ground
Eventually I left the doctoral path I had begun in China and moved to the University of Galway for a different PhD. Ireland moved my research sideways in a way I had not fully expected. Much of my earlier work was in energy economics, where the important actors were governments, industries and large institutions. Agriculture and land use brought me much closer to individual choices.
A national government can set a climate target, a model can describe a pathway, and a sector can be told that its emissions must fall. But eventually somebody owns the land. Somebody has animals to feed, bills to pay, machinery already bought, a family involved in the farm, or a good reason for continuing to do something that looks inefficient from above. That shift pulled my attention towards farmers, land-use decisions, behavioural responses and the way costs are distributed across people and places. Later, while continuing the PhD, I joined the wider FORESIGHT and FUSION research environment at Galway as a Research Assistant, which drew me further into agricultural, climate and land-use modelling.



At the Agriculture & Land Use in Ireland conference.


Research eventually gave me a community as well as a subject.
The subject had changed a great deal since accounting and my energy work, but the underlying questions had changed less than I first thought. Who makes the decision, and with what information? Which constraints are invisible from a distance? Who benefits, and who pays? What happens between a policy being designed and somebody actually having to respond to it? My doctoral work sits inside those questions. A national model may say that livestock numbers should fall, that land should change use or that a technology should be adopted. A farmer still has to decide what to do on Monday morning. The distance between the aggregate pathway and that decision has become the part of the work I care about most.
Read more about my research →

title: How I got here
text:
The people along the way
Since leaving Ghana in 2019 I have sometimes felt like a wanderer. Countries change, and so do the rooms and the people around the table. You learn new routes to work, new food, new weather, new ways of speaking, and all the small rules nobody explains because everyone else already knows them. Then, slowly, somewhere unfamiliar starts to feel ordinary.
The institutions are easy to list. The people are not. There have been classmates who became friends, colleagues who patiently explained things I probably should have known, supervisors who trusted me, people who shared meals, people who helped when I was new somewhere, and people whose paths crossed mine briefly and still left something behind. That may be the part of moving countries a CV hides best. A CV records the year you arrived. It does not record who helped make the place feel less strange.



A sunny day in Galway.


Somewhere along the way, a place you moved to for work begins collecting friendships and memories of its own.

title: How I got here
text:
Beyond the desk
Research has also given me reasons to travel. One trip took me to Washington, D.C., for the World Bank LAND Conference. The formal sessions and presentations were the reason for going, but a conference is rarely only its programme. There are the conversations afterwards, the walk through an unfamiliar city, and the things you notice that send your thinking somewhere the programme never intended. I have come to value both halves.



At the World Bank LAND Conference in Washington, D.C.


The formal programme was one part of the trip. The conversations and wandering afterwards became part of it too.
That is partly why this website is broader than my PhD. Research teaches you to narrow a question until it can be answered properly, and that discipline matters. But life keeps producing questions that do not yet fit inside a model, a journal article or a project, and I wanted somewhere to put those too. EKO Perspectives is that place. Some posts will be about agriculture or economics because that is where my research sits. Others will be about technology, science, Ghana, Africa, Ireland, a book, a place or a person. I do not expect them all to fit in one intellectual box. My own route has not.

title: How I got here
text:
Still unfinished
Writing about a journey from the middle of it has an obvious danger: accidents start to look like plans. Decisions get more credit than they deserve because their consequences only became clear years later, and memory quietly rearranges the cast. I do not want this page to become a polished origin story in which every step led neatly to the next. Some things worked and some plans changed. Some opportunities arrived unexpectedly. I walked away from one PhD and began another, and places I expected to be temporary became important parts of my life.
I will come back to this page when memory supplies something I missed, when a new chapter changes the shape of the story, or when I realise I have not thanked somebody properly. For now, this is where I am.

title: When environmental policy needs a landscape, not just a farm
text:
Agricultural fields in north County Dublin.


Photograph: C O’Flanagan / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.
Water runs downhill, and it does not consult the land registry on the way. That plain fact causes a lot of trouble for agri-environment policy. The contract is with a farmer, but the river, the hedgerow network and the invasive species the contract is meant to deal with all cross farm boundaries. A bird or a pollinator has no reason to care where one parcel ends and the next begins.



Farm boundaries are administrative. Water and habitat processes cross them.


Original schematic for EKO Perspectives.
Ireland’s Agri-Climate Rural Environment Scheme, ACRES, has started to deal with that mismatch directly. Payments still go to individual participants, as any payment scheme must, but its Co-operation approach allows some problems to be handled at a larger spatial scale. A second application window for Landscape Actions ran from 11 February to 28 May 2026, with examples including invasive species, scrub encroachment in species-rich grassland, threatened species and water-quality protection.
The experiment is not a small one. The Department describes ACRES as a €1.5 billion programme intended to support up to 50,000 farm families, and Budget 2026 reported almost 54,000 participating farmers with €280 million allocated for the year. A design change inside a scheme of that size reaches a great deal of Irish farmland.
Water quality is the clearest case for thinking beyond one holding. A farmer can change nutrient management on one farm, but the river receives the sum of what happens across the catchment. Habitat connectivity behaves in a similar way. One good patch may do little if its neighbours disappear, while several modest actions can add up once they connect. The outcome depends on a combination of decisions that are each made, and paid for, separately.
Economists will recognise the shape of this. Part of the benefit produced on one farm spills over to other farms and to the public, so the private incentive to provide it can fall short of its social value. Agri-environment payments already try to close some of that gap. Landscape coordination adds a harder problem, because the value of one farmer’s action may depend on whether neighbours act too.
Coordination carries its own costs. Someone has to define the landscape, choose the actions that suit it and judge outcomes that weather, soils and processes beyond any farmer’s control also shape. Results-based payments find this especially awkward, since the thing being rewarded is partly management and partly place. A larger planning unit can also become an excuse to assume one intervention fits everywhere inside it, and Irish farmland is too varied for that. The cost and environmental return of the same action change with soil, farm system and what happens next door.
My preference is therefore not for landscape contracts everywhere, but for starting at the scale of the environmental process. Where outcomes depend on flows or connectivity across holdings, such as catchment water quality or habitat networks, scheme design should begin with the catchment or landscape and then decide what can sensibly be delivered through individual farm contracts. Where the outcome genuinely sits within one field or holding, farm-level design may be enough. That distinction seems more useful than choosing one scale as a rule for every problem.

Elvis Kwame Ofori
Researcher and writer behind EKO Perspectives.

title: Where my PhD sits: FUSION and FORESIGHT
text:
FORESIGHT project illustration, FUSION, University of Galway, used under CC BY-SA 4.0.


Much of what I write here about Irish agriculture and climate policy comes from inside a government-funded modelling programme, and readers should know that before they read the rest.
I am doing my PhD within FUSION, the FUture Sustainable economy Integrated mOdelling Network at the University of Galway. The group works across life-cycle assessment, integrated assessment, land-use modelling and environmental software. In practice a question about agriculture does not have to stay inside an agricultural model. It can lead into forestry, energy, emissions accounting or land allocation.
Much of my work also sits alongside FORESIGHT, a project funded by Ireland’s Department of the Environment, Climate and Communications under a services contract to provide agriculture and land-use modelling to the Climate Action Modelling Group. FUSION leads the project with the University of Limerick and FERS Ltd. So when I write about Irish climate, agriculture or land-use policy, I am writing as someone who works inside a programme connected to those subjects. The views are my own and do not represent the University of Galway, the Department, funders or collaborators.
One of the tools in this environment is GOBLIN, which links agriculture, forestry and other land uses within a national land-balance framework. My own questions mostly begin after a national pathway has been made internally coherent. A national result can say that livestock, forestry or another land use changes by a given amount, but that change eventually has to meet a geography and a population of farms that differ from one another. The same national adjustment looks quite different when it reaches dairy, beef or other systems in different parts of the country. A model can be consistent in aggregate and still leave open where the transition falls, who carries it, and whether the land implied by several objectives can fit in the same places.
The habit I value most in this group is treating models as things to question. Assumptions should be visible enough to change, alternatives easy enough to test, and every result should arrive with some sense of what the model cannot tell us. Written down, that sounds like common sense. It becomes much harder to practise once a model is large and technically impressive.
The site will range well beyond my PhD, into economics, technology, Ghana, Ireland, the United States, books and code. When a post touches Irish agriculture or climate policy, though, this is the background I want readers to keep in mind.

Elvis Kwame Ofori

title: When the future is outside the data
text:
For a long time, most of my questions began with data that had already been observed. I would estimate a relationship, worry about identification, and then ask what the result implied for policy. Econometrics deals in counterfactuals all the time, so the method was never confined to the past. What changed during my PhD was the distance. Some of the futures I was asked to think about sat far outside anything the data had seen.
Distance matters because an estimate is most trustworthy close to the variation that produced it. Push far enough beyond that range and the regression still returns a number, but more of the answer now comes from the functional form and less from anything observed. That is not a flaw in econometrics. It is a boundary, and large policy questions make it easy to see.
The Irish Land Use Review shows the kind of question I mean. Its scenarios include substantial additional forestry and large-scale rewetting of grassland on organic soils by 2050. Those are not year-to-year movements in a land system. They change the structure of the system itself, and no record of past farm decisions was collected under that structure.



Irish farm field. Photograph by Daniel Hanrahan.


Source: Daniel Hanrahan / Wikimedia Commons, used under CC BY 3.0.
Scenario modelling approaches the problem from the other end. A scenario starts from a target, a policy assumption or a possible condition and asks what else would have to change if that condition held. Backcasting goes further, beginning at the future objective and working back towards the present. The European Commission’s short guide to scenario building in foresight and the OECD’s strategic foresight work draw the same line between exploring plausible futures and predicting one.
Observed behaviour stays essential inside a scenario. If the scenario assumes that farms respond to a price, a payment or a constraint in a particular way, past behaviour is still the best discipline on that assumption. The mistake is letting a historical estimate carry the whole exercise once the system has moved well beyond the conditions that produced it.
My own view is that every scenario result should come with a plain statement of which numbers were estimated and which were assumed. It is a small reporting habit, and it would make many land-use results far easier to read. A reader could then decide how far to trust the extrapolation instead of discovering it in an appendix.
Climate policy has an older version of the same division. An OECD paper on emissions baselines separates top-down economic models, which give economy-wide coherence, from bottom-up technology and sector models, which give detail. I now think about my own methods in similar terms. Econometrics tells me what observed variation can teach. Scenario models ask what a different future would require. Spatial models ask where the change lands. Microsimulation stops me forgetting that thousands of farms facing one policy will not respond in one way.
No single method does all of that well, and I have stopped looking for one that claims to.

Elvis Kwame Ofori
Researcher and writer behind EKO Perspectives.

title: A map can clarify the world and still leave something out
text:
A 1905 Ordnance Survey Ireland map of Dunfanaghy and surrounding land in County Donegal.


Ordnance Survey Ireland, six-inch Donegal Sheet 15, published 1905. Director General of the Ordnance Survey Office, Dublin; digital image via the National Library of Scotland and Wikimedia Commons. Underlying map public domain; digital image CC BY 4.0.
The map above is the 1905 edition of Ordnance Survey sheet 15 for County Donegal, covering Horn Head and the town of Dunfanaghy. Nearly half the sheet is open Atlantic. Around the town, field boundaries are packed tightly together; on the higher ground behind it they thin out into scattered symbols for rough land. It is a careful and accurate piece of work, and it records exactly what the survey was built to record: boundaries, roads, buildings and heights. Who worked which field, on what terms, and how the hill ground was used are not on it, because the map was never designed to carry them.
James C. Scott’s Seeing Like a State is about the gap between a map like this and the world it describes. The book is usually read as a critique of large schemes of social improvement, and it moves through scientific forestry, cadastral maps, urban planning, collectivisation, villagisation and agricultural modernisation. The thread running through them is what Scott calls legibility: complicated social and ecological worlds translated into categories that institutions can count, compare and administer.



A complex landscape becomes a smaller set of model categories. The simplification makes comparison possible, but some information disappears.


Original schematic for EKO Perspectives.
Legibility is not foolish. A forest can be represented as timber volume, land divided into mapped parcels, people counted in a census, farms classified as dairy, cattle, sheep, tillage or mixed. A government that cannot identify property, measure resources or count people will struggle to tax, plan services or run a policy at all. Scott’s warning is narrower than a rejection of measurement, and more useful. Trouble begins when the representation starts to stand in for the thing it represents.
His forestry example shows how. A forest managed around a narrow measure of timber production can look admirably ordered while losing ecological relationships the accounts never valued. A planned settlement can make sense on paper and work badly for people whose movements, trades and ties were never visible in the plan. The simplification makes intervention possible, and it can hide some of the knowledge the intervention needs.
Modelling lives on the same ground, which is why I keep returning to the book. Models depend on legibility too. We choose variables, harmonise categories, build representative units, aggregate activities and draw boundaries around systems. A spatial model divides a continuous landscape into units. A microsimulation assigns people or farms to types. Scenario thinking turns an uncertain future into a manageable set of assumptions. None of this is a defect. It is what makes modelling possible in the first place.
The tempting answer is more detail, and it is usually the wrong one. Complexity is not realism. A model with a thousand weakly identified parameters can hide more than a transparent model with twenty, and policy needs shared categories anyway, since a programme cannot be administered if every case has its own private definition. The better habit is to ask, every time, what the simplification cannot see.
Take a land-use model that finds the least-cost spatial arrangement for meeting an emissions target. The optimisation can be internally correct and still leave important questions outside it. Who owns the land selected for change? Are there tenure constraints? Does the model see labour at all? Are two hectares that look interchangeable in the data actually different because of soil, fragmentation, access or local markets? Does the transition rely on behaviour that was assumed rather than observed? Asking these does not make the model useless. It defines the claim the model can support.
Scott gives real weight to practical knowledge, which he discusses through the Greek term mētis: knowledge built up through experience and adaptation to local conditions, and often hard to formalise. Agricultural analysis has an obvious version of it. Administrative data may say two farms have the same area and enterprise type, while a farmer or adviser sees at once that they differ in soil, family labour, machinery, succession, fragmentation or access to markets. The task is not to choose local knowledge over formal evidence. It is to notice when one is quietly being asked to substitute for the other.
That is what stays with me from the book. Standardising the world makes some things visible by pushing others out of view, and a model is useful precisely because it does this on purpose. The discipline lies in being just as deliberate about what has disappeared.

Elvis Kwame Ofori
Researcher and writer behind EKO Perspectives.

title: AI is becoming ordinary. The evidence about its effects is still catching up
text:
Two students spend thirty minutes with the same AI model. One asks for the answer and copies it. The other attempts the problem first, asks for criticism, argues with the response and revises the work. A study that records both as thirty minutes of AI use has measured time well and behaviour badly.



The same amount of AI exposure can conceal very different learning behaviour.


Original schematic for EKO Perspectives.
I had those two students in mind while reading OpenAI’s call for research on AI and teen development. On 8 September 2026, the company announced $5 million for independent research on how generative AI affects people aged 13 to 17. The call asks about emotional development, relationships, patterns of use, safeguards, AI literacy and differences across social and cultural settings. Those are better questions than the one public debate keeps returning to, which is whether AI is good or bad for learning.
The funding source matters. A company developing the technology has an institutional interest in the evidence that grows up around it, which makes independence, disclosure, publication and replication important. The call requires conflict disclosures, lists independence and credibility among its review criteria and encourages public release of findings. Whether that proves enough will depend on what gets published, including results the funder would rather not see.
Early evidence needs the same care. A 2026 meta-analysis in Humanities and Social Sciences Communications reported generally positive pooled effects of generative-AI-supported approaches on outcomes including academic achievement, higher-order thinking and writing. It is a reasonable place to start. A pooled estimate, though, averages over many designs, and it cannot say which of my two students drove the result unless the underlying studies recorded what students actually did. The intervention, the subject, the learner, the comparison group, study quality and the role the system played all sit inside that one number.
Timing is a second difficulty. Models improve, interfaces change, safeguards are added and users learn new habits, sometimes between a study’s design and its publication. A rigorous result can become historically specific quickly. Social scientists are used to treatments that drift, but generative AI compresses the timetable.
I am therefore cautious with studies that reduce exposure to time spent with a tool or mere access to it, especially when they do not record how the system was used. Those measures can still tell us something, but they cannot distinguish between AI replacing an attempt, supplying feedback after an attempt, or supporting revision. Studies that capture the pattern of use give us a better chance of understanding the mechanism. The same applies to outcomes: exam performance, long-term retention, writing quality, confidence, reasoning and time saved are not interchangeable measures of learning.
For universities and schools, that leaves neither the blanket ban nor the blanket embrace on very solid evidential ground. The same issue will turn up outside education. A model can score extremely well on a benchmark and produce a much smaller effect once people reorganise their work around it. The unit worth studying is often not the model alone, but the working arrangement between a person and a machine.

Elvis Kwame Ofori
Researcher and writer behind EKO Perspectives.

Ireland’s fire season comes in spring. The Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine’s fire-management page identifies a spring fire-risk season, and when I checked it in late September 2026 it listed three Fire Danger Notices for the year. The photograph above, of gorse and heather burning on a Cork hillside, is an Irish version of the problem. It looks nothing like a Mediterranean forest fire, and much of what shapes the risk on a hillside like that is settled before an emergency begins.
That is also the argument running through the European Commission’s Communication on Integrated Wildfire Risk Management, adopted on 25 March 2026. The strategy treats prevention, preparedness, response and recovery as parts of one system, and its guidance for agriculture and forests gives farmers and foresters a role throughout. Grazing, agroforestry, thinning, firebreaks and other land management shape fuel loads and landscape structure well before an ignition.



Wildfire policy is a cycle, not only an emergency response.


Original schematic for EKO Perspectives.
Ireland is not southern Europe, and importing the Mediterranean fire story wholesale would mislead. Irish guidance already treats wildfire as more than a firefighting problem, though. The Office of Emergency Planning names peatlands, turf-cutting bogs, uplands and immature forest among the land most prone to wildfire, and notes that active farming, appropriate grazing and other fuel reduction can lower the risk. Teagasc’s guidance for forest owners stresses fire plans, maintained firebreaks, access routes, water sources and cooperation with neighbouring landowners. None of it looks dramatic beside aircraft, fire engines or an evacuation, and all of it has to be done before the emergency to count for anything.
Neighbours appear in that guidance for a reason. The benefits and risks of managing land for fire do not stop at a property boundary. A well-managed parcel can reduce fuel across a wider area, while a blocked access route or an unmanaged strip creates problems next door. Fire prevention therefore shares the coordination problem that runs through water quality, biodiversity and invasive-species policy: the ecological unit is often larger than the holding through which policy is paid.
My view is that, on uplands and the margins of peatland, wildfire prevention belongs partly inside ordinary land-management policy, alongside emergency planning rather than in opposition to it. Grazing, access, vegetation management and agri-environment measures can shape risk before ignition; emergency services remain essential once a fire starts. That does not mean managing every landscape the same way. Peatlands and habitats have their own ecological objectives, and badly designed fuel reduction can damage the things a policy is meant to protect. Prescribed burning, where it is used at all, needs expertise, legal compliance and careful timing.
Nor is a plausible mechanism the same as demonstrated effect. Grazing reduces some fuels, but the result depends on stocking, vegetation, season, terrain and the ecosystem in question. Bringing fire prevention into land-management policy only works if those schemes ask where an intervention works, at what intensity and cost, and with what consequences for biodiversity, carbon and farming.
By the time a hillside is burning, many of those choices have already been made, but that makes prevention and emergency response parts of the same system rather than substitutes for one another.

Elvis Kwame Ofori

title: Research
text:
My research asks a distributional question:
I use spatial, economic and behavioural modelling to connect national pathways with the local realities through which they must be implemented.

title: Research
text:
Current work
GOBLIN-Spatial
When Ireland’s national land-use pathway says livestock numbers fall and land changes use, where in the country does that happen, and does everything the plan asks of the land actually fit?
BioLand-US
Models say where the United States could grow perennial energy crops. BioLand-US asks how much of that land is suitable and how much farmers would actually sign up through voluntary contracts.
IFT-BioSim
The same national target costs different farms very different amounts. IFT-BioSim models those costs farm by farm, and tests whether different support designs change who bears them.

title: Research
text:
Methods
My work uses econometrics, spatial modelling, optimisation, synthetic populations and microsimulation, implemented mainly in Python, R, Stata, GIS and SQL.

title: BioLand-US
text:
Energy-crop models can say where perennial biomass could be grown in the United States. They cannot say whether farmers will sign up. BioLand-US sits between those two things and asks a practical implementation question:

When a techno-economic model allocates land to perennial biomass, how much of that prospective allocation can also be supported by compatible agricultural land and voluntary contractual participation?

The model does not replace or re-optimise the upstream resource allocation. It adds an explicit implementation layer.

title: BioLand-US
text:
Scientific logic
The framework keeps four quantities distinct:





flowchart TD
    A["Techno-economic biomass allocation"] --> B["Compatible agricultural land"]
    B --> C["Contractually accessible land"]
    C --> D["Prospectively mobilised biomass"]






This makes it possible to distinguish technical allocation from land compatibility and actual access through voluntary contracts.

title: GOBLIN-Spatial
text:
Ireland’s national plans for agriculture and land use can say how much livestock numbers fall and how much land changes use. They do not say where. GOBLIN-Spatial is about the where.
National AFOLU (agriculture, forestry and other land use) pathways can specify how livestock numbers, land release and future land uses change without showing where those changes fall.
GOBLIN-Spatial asks:

When a nationally coherent agricultural transition requires restructuring, where does transition pressure concentrate, what can the released land support, and can competing future land-use requirements be accommodated within the available geography?

GOBLIN supplies the national pathway. GOBLIN-Spatial resolves its geography and tests spatial feasibility.

title: GOBLIN-Spatial
text:
How it works





flowchart TD
    A["National GOBLIN pathway"] --> B["Transition incidence<br/>Where does adjustment fall?"]
    B --> C["Spatial response potential<br/>What can released land support?"]
    C --> D["Spatial transformability<br/>Can competing future land uses fit?"]
    D --> E["Spatial flexibility<br/>Is one geography necessary?"]






The framework is a spatial stress-test of transition pathways, not a prediction of individual farmer or parcel decisions.

title: GOBLIN-Spatial
text:
Evidence and scale
The historical reconstruction covers 2015–2025 and is anchored to the 2020 Census of Agriculture at Electoral Division level. Higher-level livestock controls maintain national accounting consistency while preserving validated local structure.
The model combines agricultural statistics with land, soil and drainage information, LPIS context and explicit eligibility controls.

title: GOBLIN-Spatial
GOBLIN-Spatial
text:
What it does not claim
The model does not predict individual farmer behaviour, household welfare, market prices, parcel-level adoption or the exact geography that will exist in 2050.
Those questions require behavioural, farm-level or market models.
